## Wrangling: tidy, then transform

::: {.notes}
Warn participants not to knit/render: it takes too long on Renku. We execute the code as it is presented.
:::

![](images/fig-data-wrangling.png){fig-alt="The data science pipeline, with the Tidy and Transform steps highlighted: data wrangling covers both." width="80%" fig-align="center"}

-   **Tidy**: clean the data into **tidy tables** (`tibbles`)
-   **Transform**: reshape it to get insight

Both are **data wrangling**.

## Basic wrangling tasks

-   **Pick columns** from a table
-   **Pick rows**: subsetting
-   **Transform** or **add** columns
-   **Order** the rows
-   **Group** the rows, to compute within groups
-   Compute **summary statistics**

. . .

`{dplyr}` and `{tidyr}`: a whole **grammar** to manipulate data.

# A Grammar for Data Manipulation {#DataManip .subsection background-color="#425556"}

## `{dplyr}`: verbs to wrangle data {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap='The pliers of `{dplyr}` will help us wrangle our data!', fig.align='center', out.width = "90%", fig.alt="The hexagonal logo of the dplyr package: a pair of pliers."}
#| label: img-dplyr-logo
knitr::include_graphics(path = "images/hex-dplyr.png")
```
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
|           Verb            | Use                                                                                                 |
|:-----------------:|-----------------------------------------------------|
|        `select()`         | **pick a set of columns** from a `tibble`                                                           |
|        `filter()`         | **pick a set of rows**                                                                              |
|        `mutate()`         | **transform and add columns** to the `tibble`                                                       |
|        `arrange()`        | **order the rows** according to the values of a (set of) column(s)                                  |
|       `group_by()`        | **group** according to the values of a (set of) column(s) to perform calculations within the groups |
| `summarise()/summarize()` | create a new `tibble` containing **summary statistics** for a set of columns                        |
:::
::::

## Verbs chain into sentences

::: callout-important
## Why "verbs"?

-   **First argument**: the **dataset**
-   **Other arguments**: the **columns**

So, with the **pipe**, they chain into sentences:

``` r
select(dataset, column_1, column_2)

# Is equivalent to:

dataset %>% select(column_1, column_2)

# you see that it reads like a sentence!
```

:::

## Inspecting Data

Right after importing, check:

-   **Which columns** are in the dataset
-   Their **types**: numbers (`integer`, `double`), text (`character`), `logical` (`TRUE`/`FALSE`), dates...
-   Where the **missing values** (`NA`) are

## The WTA dataset {.smaller}

Women's tennis: one row per **Grand Slam match**.

::: callout-note
-   The path goes **one level up**, to the workshop's shared `data` folder (`../data/`)
-   The path is *fed* to `read_csv()` with the pipe `%>%`

:::

```{r}
#| label: read-wta
library(readr)

wta_data <-
  "../data/wta_grand_slam_data.csv" %>%
  read_csv(
    col_types = cols(.default = "c")
    )
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A note on the extra arguments

-   `col_types = cols(.default = "c")` imports **every column as text** (`"c"` for `character`)
-   `read_csv()` *guesses* the types from the first 1000 lines: columns with many `NA` can be guessed wrong

:::

## Inspecting: the first rows with `slice_head()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: slice-head-wta
slice_head(wta_data)
```

More rows? Set the argument `n`:

```{r}
#| label: slice-head-wta-6
slice_head(wta_data, n = 6)
```

## Inspecting: a summary with `glimpse()` {.smaller .scrollable}

-   One line per column: **name**, **type** and the first values

```{r}
#| label: glimpse-wta
glimpse(wta_data)
```

## The columns of the WTA data

`r ncol(wta_data)` columns, grouped by **prefix**:

| column / prefix | Content                                                                        |
|:-----------------:|:----------------------------------------------------|
|     `year`      | Year of the tournament the match took place                                    |
|   `tourney_*`   | Information related to the tournament (`id`, `name`, `surface`, ...)           |
|   `match_num`   | Number of match **within a tournament**                                        |
|   `winner_*`    | Information related to the winner of a given match (`id`, `name`, `hand`, ...) |
|    `loser_*`    | Information related to the loser of a given match (`id`, `name`, `hand`, ...)  |

## Inspecting: the full picture with `vis_dat()`

-   **Colours**: the column **types** · **Grey**: **missing** values

```{r, fig.cap = "A bird's-eye view of the WTA dataset using `vis_dat()`"}
#| label: vis-dat-wta
#| output-location: column
#| fig-alt: "vis_dat() plot of the WTA data: one vertical band per column, all coloured as character, with grey blocks marking missing values, which are frequent in some columns."
library(visdat)
wta_data %>%
  vis_dat(
    # `warn_large_data = FALSE` added to avoid warnings
    warn_large_data = FALSE
    )
```

## Cleaning column names with `{janitor}` {.smaller}

-   Files prepared by people: spaces, capitals, units in brackets...
-   `clean_names()` rewrites **all** names in lower-case `snake_case`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: read-team-bad-names
team <- read_csv("data/team_bad_names.csv")
team
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: clean-names-team
library(janitor)
team %>%
  clean_names()
```
:::
::::

::: callout-tip
## Why bother?

Quicker to type, **no backticks**, RStudio **autocompletes** them. Call `clean_names()` once, right after importing.

:::

## Picking columns with `select()`

-   **One column**, by its name:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#| label: select-year
wta_data %>%
  select(year)
```

-   **Several columns**: list their names

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#| label: select-columns
wta_data %>%
  select(year, tourney_id, tourney_name, winner_id, winner_name)
```

## `select()` with selection helpers

-   Pick the columns **whose names fulfil a condition**, e.g. `starts_with()`

```{r}
#| label: select-helpers
#| output-location: column
#| fig-alt: "vis_dat() plot of the selected columns: year, then the winner_ and tourney_ columns, all of type character."
wta_data %>%
  select(year, starts_with("winner"), starts_with("tourney")) %>%
  vis_dat(warn_large_data = FALSE)
```

## Other selection helpers

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Other Selection Helpers

Most of the other selection helpers have almost self-explanatory names, e.g.

| Selection Helper | Use case                                                                                                                       |
|:----------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------|
|  `ends_with()`   | selects according to a suffix                                                                                                  |
|   `contains()`   | when we are looking for columns that contain a literal word or string                                                          |
|   `matches()`    | selects according to **patterns known as regular expressions** (see [R's documentation on regular expressions](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/regex.html)) |
|  `num_range()`   | selects columns numbered in a range, e.g. `x10`, `x11`, ..., `x15` with `num_range("x", 10:15)`                                 |

Other selection helpers apply to vectors of column names, such as `all_of()` and `any_of()`, and finally `where()`, which selects according to a function.
:::

## Transforming columns with `mutate()`

-   **Create** new columns or **transform** existing ones
-   Here: `year` → **number**, `tourney_date` → **date** (`ymd()` from `{lubridate}`)

```{r}
#| label: mutate-types
#| output-location: column
#| fig-alt: "vis_dat() plot of the selected columns after mutate(): year is now numeric and tourney_date is a date, the other columns are still character."
library(lubridate)

wta_data <-
  wta_data %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    tourney_date = ymd(tourney_date))

wta_data %>%
  select(year, starts_with("winner"), starts_with("tourney")) %>%
  vis_dat(warn_large_data = FALSE)
```

## Making the changes permanent

::: callout-important
## Making permanent changes to a table

We **assigned** the result back to `wta_data`: the original table is **rewritten**.

The following pipe **does not modify** the contents of `data` **permanently**:

``` r
data %>% mutate(...)
```

The following pipe **does modify** the contents of `data` **permanently**:

``` r
data <- data %>% mutate(...)
```
:::

## Sub-setting rows with `filter()` {.smaller}

-   Keep the rows that **fulfil a logical condition**
-   E.g. the matches won by Serena Williams:

```{r}
#| label: filter-serena
wta_data %>%
  select(year, starts_with("winner"), starts_with("tourney")) %>%
  filter(winner_name == "Serena Williams")
```

::: callout-important
## Assignment (`=`) vs Comparison (`==`)

Comparison uses the **double** equal sign `==`. The single `=` assigns, e.g. in `mutate()`.

:::

## `filter()` with several conditions {.smaller}

-   Rows must fulfil **all** the conditions
-   `str_detect()` (`{stringr}`): `TRUE` when the text **contains a pattern**

```{r}
#| label: filter-serena-australian
library(stringr)
wta_data %>%
  filter(
    winner_name == "Serena Williams",
    str_detect(tourney_name, pattern = "Australian"))
```

## How to write logical conditions {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to write logical conditions

Here's a quick rundown on how to write logical conditions in R:

|       Logical Condition        |  Symbol  |
|:------------------------------:|:--------:|
|         *A equal to B*         | `A == B` |
|        *A less than B*         | `A < B`  |
|   *A less than or equal to B*  | `A <= B` |
|       *A greater than B*       | `A > B`  |
|   *A greater or equal to B*    | `A >= B` |

One can also combine conditions into longer statements with "and" and "or":

|       Logical Condition       |          Syntax           |
|:-----------------------------:|:-------------------------:|
| *Condition 1 AND Condition 2* | `ConditionA & ConditionB` |
| *Condition 1 OR Condition 2*  | `ConditionA | ConditionB` |

Finally, a very handy shortcut for multiple `OR` conditions is the `%in%` operator, which compares a value to the contents of a vector. For instance:

    A == B | A == C | A == D

is equivalent to:

    A %in% c(B, C, D)
:::

## Sort observations with `arrange()` {.smaller}

-   **Numbers**: increasing order · **Text**: alphabetical order

```{r}
#| label: arrange-year
#| output-location: column
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>%
  arrange(year)
```

```{r}
#| label: arrange-winner-name
#| output-location: column
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>%
  arrange(winner_name)
```

## `arrange()`: several columns, descending order {.smaller}

-   Sorts by the **first** column, then by the **second**...
-   `desc()` reverses the order

```{r}
#| label: arrange-two-columns
#| output-location: column
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>%
  arrange(year, winner_name)
```

```{r}
#| label: arrange-desc
#| output-location: column
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>%
  arrange(year, desc(winner_name))
```

## Producing summary statistics with `summarise()`

-   Creates a **new table** with **summaries** of the columns
-   `n()` **counts the rows**: how many Australian matches did Serena win?

```{r}
#| label: summarise-serena-australian
wta_data %>%
  filter(
    winner_name == "Serena Williams",
    str_detect(tourney_name, pattern = "Australian")) %>%
  summarise(number_of_wins = n())
```

## Other summary functions

| Summary Statistic | Functions                      |
|:-----------------:|:-------------------------------|
|      Center       | `mean()`, `median()`           |
|      Spread       | `sd()`, `IQR()`, `mad()`       |
|       Range       | `min()`, `max()`, `quantile()` |
|     Position      | `first()`, `last()`, `nth()`   |
|       Count       | `n()`, `n_distinct()`          |
|      Logical      | `any()`, `all()`               |

## Creating groups with `group_by()` {.smaller}

-   **Groups** the rows by the values of one or more columns
-   The printout shows the **groups**: later computations happen **within** them

```{r}
#| label: group-by-winner
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name)
```

## Removing the groups with `ungroup()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: ungroup-winner
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name) %>%
  ungroup()
```

## Computing summaries within groups with `group_by()` `%>%` `summarise()` {.smaller}

-   `summarise()` after `group_by()`: **one row per group**
-   The number of wins of **every** player:

```{r}
#| label: wins-per-player
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name) %>%
  summarise(number_of_wins = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

::: callout-note
## What does `.groups = "drop"` do?

It returns a table **without groups**, as if we had added `ungroup()`. A forgotten grouping is a common source of surprises!

:::

## A shortcut for counting: `count()` {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A shortcut for counting: `count()`

Counting the rows within groups is so common that `{dplyr}` has a shortcut for it. `count()` groups, counts and ungroups in one step:

```{r}
#| label: count-wins-per-player
wta_data %>%
  count(winner_name, name = "number_of_wins")
```
:::

## Grouping by several columns {.smaller}

The wins of **each player** in **each tournament**:

```{r}
#| label: wins-per-player-tourney
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name, tourney_name) %>%
  summarise(number_of_wins = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

# Merging Data {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## Binding and joining

-   Real data is often split into **several linked tables**
-   To get the information we need, we **merge** them

|     Verb      | Use                                                                          |
|:-----------------:|-----------------------------------------------------|
| `bind_rows()` | merges two tibbles by **stacking them up** (one on top of the other)         |
|  `*_join()`   | **attaches** tibbles by **the columns they have in common** (joining *keys*) |

## Three toy datasets {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: toy-datasets
data_1 <- tibble(id = 1:3, var_1 = c(15, 13, 39))
data_2 <- tibble(id = c(4, 5), var_1 = 10)
data_3 <- tibble(id = 1:3, var_2 = c(10, 12, 14), var_3 = c(45, 20, 2))
```

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
#| label: print-data-1
data_1
```
::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
#| label: print-data-2
data_2
```
::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
#| label: print-data-3
data_3
```
::::
:::::

## *Stacking* data sets with `bind_rows()`

-   **Same columns**, **different rows**: stack them up
-   The left-hand side of the pipe goes **on top**

```{r}
#| label: bind-rows-data
data_1 %>%
  bind_rows(data_2)
```

## *Joining* data sets with `left_join()`

-   **Same rows**, **different columns**: attach the columns
-   The `*_join()` verbs: `left_join()`, `right_join()`, `full_join()`...
-   They match the rows by a **common column**: the **joining key**

## Wait! Isn't there a `bind_cols()`? {.smaller .scrollable}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Wait! Isn't there a `bind_cols()`?

Yes there is! But it's a function that does not ensure **row consistency**. We can illustrate some of the problems with an example.

-   For example, `data_3` contains the same ids as `data_1`, hence we can attach the values of the columns `var_2` and `var_3` to have a more complete dataset.

```{r}
#| label: bind-cols-data
data_1 %>%
  bind_cols(select(data_3, starts_with("var")))
```

Success! ... or is it?

There are a couple of drawbacks when using `bind_cols()`:

1.  **It does not verify the conformity of the rows**.

    For instance, a simple permutation in one of the datasets, or a lack of conformity in terms of rows, entails problems.

    -   Let's see what happens when the data in `data_3` is permuted, e.g. in the descending order of `id`.
    -   Carrying out the merge with `bind_cols()` yields an inconsistent result!

```{r}
#| label: permute-data-3
data_3 <- data_3 %>% arrange(desc(id))
```

```{r}
#| label: bind-cols-permuted
data_1 %>%
  bind_cols(select(data_3, starts_with("var")))
```

2.  The tibbles you want to merge **must have the same number of rows**.
    -   Suppose we want to merge our three datasets to have all the information in one tibble.
    -   The first two can be merged using `bind_rows()`.
    -   Yet, when we attempt (wrongly!) to merge (the permuted!) `data_3`, we get an error message.
    -   This is because we have 5 rows in the first dataset and 3 in the second!

```{r, error=TRUE}
#| label: bind-cols-error
data_1 %>%
  bind_rows(data_2) %>%
  bind_cols(data_3)
```

Using the `*_join` verbs of `{dplyr}`, we ensure the consistency of the rows.
:::

## How `left_join()` works

![](images/left-join.gif){fig-alt="Animation of left_join(x, y): the rows of y are matched to the rows of x by their shared key column, the columns of y are attached to x, and the rows of x without a match get missing values." width="45%" fig-align="center"}

**Source:** [Garrick Aden-Buie's](https://github.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain) Tidy Animated Verbs

::: callout-important
## Why the "left" in `left_join()`?

It also **keeps the rows of the first** (*left-hand side*) **tibble** that have no match.

:::

## `left_join()` with a joining key {.smaller}

-   Default: joins on **all** the shared columns
-   `by` picks the key: `by = "id"` (or `by = join_by(id)` in recent `{dplyr}`)

```{r}
#| label: left-join-id
data_1 %>%
  bind_rows(data_2) %>%
  left_join(data_3, by = "id")
```

## Rows without a match {.smaller}

`data_4`: `data_3` plus a row with `id = 8`, which isn't in `data_1`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: data-4
data_4 <- bind_rows(data_3, tibble(id = 8, var_2 = 3, var_3 = 12))
data_4
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| label: left-join-unmatched
data_1 %>%
  left_join(data_4, by = "id")
```
:::
::::

# Pivoting Data {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## Long vs wide tables

-   **Long**: every column is a *variable* → for **analysis** (computations, plots)
-   **Wide**: some columns are named after *values* of a variable → for **display** in reports

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap='Wide-format vs. long-format data', fig.align='center', out.width = "70%", fig.alt="The same data as a wide table, with an id column and one column each for x, y and z, and as a long table with three columns: id, key (holding x, y or z) and val."}
#| label: img-wide-long
knitr::include_graphics("images/original-dfs-tidy.png")
```

## `{tidyr}`: `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap='The brooms of `{tidyr}` will help us tidy our data!', fig.align='center', out.width = "90%", fig.alt="The hexagonal logo of the tidyr package: brooms."}
#| label: img-tidyr-logo
knitr::include_graphics(path = "images/hex-tidyr.png")
```
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
![](images/tidyr-longer-wider.gif){fig-alt="Animation of a wide table turned into a long table with pivot_longer(), and back into a wide table with pivot_wider()." width="480"}

Source: [Garrick Aden-Buie's](https://github.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain) Tidy Animated Verbs, modified by [Mara Averick](https://twitter.com/dataandme)
:::
::::

## Pivoting into long-form with `pivot_longer()`

|  Argument   | Use                                                                                    |
|:----------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------|
|   `cols`    | the **columns to convert** into a single column                                        |
| `names_to`  | the **name of a new column**, where the **names of the selected columns** are stored   |
| `values_to` | the **name of the column** where we store **the values**                               |

Typical case: **measurements repeated over time**, one column per timepoint.

## From wide to long {.smaller}

Prototypes measured at 3 timepoints → one `timepoint` column, one `performance` column

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: data-5-wide
data_5_wide <-
  tibble(
    prototype = 1:5 ,
    t_1 = c(12,1,3,4,5),
    t_2 = c(13,0,3,6,3),
    t_3 = c(14,-1,3,8,1))
data_5_wide
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: pivot-longer
data_5_long <-
  data_5_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(prototype), # means: selecting all but the prototype column
    names_to = "timepoint",
    values_to = "performance"
  )

data_5_long
```
:::
::::

## Optional: cleaner timepoints {.smaller}

-   `names_prefix` drops the `t_` prefix, `names_transform` makes the timepoint a **number**

```{r}
#| label: pivot-longer-clean
#| output-location: column
data_5_long <-
  data_5_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(prototype),
    names_to = "timepoint",
    values_to = "performance",
    names_prefix = "t_", # to remove the `t_` prefix
    names_transform = list(timepoint = as.integer) # to transform the timepoints into integers
  )

data_5_long
```

## Long tables are made for computing

The average performance of every prototype:

```{r}
#| label: average-performance
data_5_long %>%
  group_by(prototype) %>%
  summarise(average_performance = mean(performance), .groups = "drop")
```

## Pivoting into wide-form with `pivot_wider()`

-   The opposite of `pivot_longer()`: **spreads** the values of a column into **new columns**
-   Wide tables are good for **presentation**, e.g. in reports

|   Argument    | Use                                                                            |
|:-----------------:|:----------------------------------------------------|
| `names_from`  | the column whose contents become the names of the new columns                  |
| `values_from` | the column from which the function *fetches* the values for the new columns    |

## From long to wide {.smaller}

**Average yields** of **crops** by **agricultural practice**: the repeated values make it hard to read

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: data-6-long
data_6_long <-
  tibble(
    crop = c(rep("wheat", 3), rep("corn", 3), rep("quinoa",3)),
    practice = rep(c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3"), 3),
    yield = c(12,65,85,98, 65, 45, 72, 67, 59)
    )
data_6_long
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}

## Presentation-ready with `{kableExtra}`

```{r}
#| label: pivot-wider-kable
library(kableExtra)
data_6_long %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = practice, values_from = yield) %>%
  kbl(caption = "Table 1: Yields of crops according to agricultural practices") %>%
  kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria")
```
